title: Spanner Deep Dive
description: Explore Google Spanner's TrueTime API, commit-wait protocol, and how it achieves globally consistent reads across data centers.

segments.text: Google Spanner is the database that broke the rules. It provides both strong consistency AND global distribution. The secret ingredient? Atomic clocks. Let's understand how.

In a distributed database spanning continents, clocks on different machines drift apart. If server A's clock says 10:00:00 and server B says 10:00:05, you cannot use timestamps to order transactions. Consistency breaks.

TrueTime does not give you a single timestamp. It gives you an interval: earliest and latest possible times. The interval accounts for clock uncertainty. TrueTime guarantees the real time falls within this interval.

Google achieves tight intervals using GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data center. GPS gives microsecond accuracy, atomic clocks handle GPS outages. The uncertainty window is typically one to seven milliseconds.

segments.thought_prompt: If timestamps have uncertainty intervals, how can Spanner guarantee that transaction A's timestamp is definitively before transaction B's?

segments.text: Commit-wait. After assigning a commit timestamp, Spanner waits until the uncertainty interval has passed before making the transaction visible. This guarantees that no other server could assign an earlier timestamp to a later transaction.

This achieves external consistency, also called linearizability. If transaction T1 commits before T2 starts in real time, T1's timestamp is guaranteed to be less than T2's. The global order matches real-world causality.

Read-only transactions are lock-free. Pick a read timestamp, find a replica whose data is sufficiently up to date, and read. No coordination needed. This is why Spanner reads scale globally without bottlenecks.

Each shard is replicated using Paxos for consensus. Writes go through a Paxos leader. Cross-shard transactions use two-phase commit coordinated by a transaction manager. Strong consistency with high availability.

Spanner uses a relational model with SQL support, interleaved tables for parent-child co-location, and automatic sharding by primary key ranges. It feels like a traditional RDBMS but operates at planet scale.

segments.thought_prompt: Commit-wait adds latency equal to the clock uncertainty. What happens if GPS fails and uncertainty grows to 100ms?

segments.text: Latency increases proportionally. That is why Google invests heavily in clock infrastructure. Spanner proved that you can have strong consistency globally if you invest in time synchronization. It changed how we think about distributed databases forever.
